Colonoscopy with biopsy for tissue diagnosis examines the entire colon and is the preferred initial test for patients with suspected colon cancer. C

background.definition: A malignant neoplasm that occurs in the colon or rectum (60% distal colon, 40% proximal colon). Adenocarcinoma is the most common histologic cell type. Carcinoid and squamous cell carcinoma are uncommon histologic types, and melanoma occurs rarely.

Third most common cause of cancer and third leading cause of cancer-related death
An accumulation of mutational events and complex molecular changes evolves into successive changes from normal colonic mucosa to adenomatous polyp to adenocarcinoma.
Diet is an important environmental factor. Obesity is strongly associated with increased risk of early onset CRC.

Specific genetic disorders (familial adenomatous polyposis and hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) are associated with a high risk of developing colon cancer. There is a PCR test to screen for non-polyposis CRC.
Inflammatory bowel disease carries an increased risk of CRC proportional to the extent and duration of disease. Patients with myotonic muscular dystrophy are also at increased risk.

Irritable bowel syndrome is not associated with increased risk of CRC. On analysis of the 22,000 (5%) patients in a UK biobank with IBS, they had reduced incidence and reduced cancer specific mortality from CRC.
Most CRCs arise from preexisting adenomatous polyps.
It takes more than 10 years for an adenomatous polyp to become cancerous.
K-ras oncogene is frequently (40%-50%) implicated in CRC.
Mutated suppressor genes on chromosomes 17,18 frequently (75%) seen.

Five histologic factors of polyps identified in patients with T1 CRC have a higher risk of metastasis: lymphovascular invasion, Haggitt level 4, muscularis mucosa type B, poorly differentiated clusters, tumor budding.
5-microRNA identifies high risk T1 CRC better than current pathologic identifiers.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Current moderate to heavy alcohol use
Certain oral bacteria types may increase or decrease risk of CRC.
CRC risk calculation model that includes genetic, environmental and family history predicts risk better than risk calculation model that only includes family history.
A Swedish study found that the risk of CRC is significantly increased in first-degree relatives of persons with CRC (4% in the general population, 6% with one first degree relative, and 9% with two).

list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening average-risk adults age 45 to 75 years using any of the following: annual FOBTs, annual FIT test; FIT-DNA every 1 to 3 years; colonoscopy every 10 years; CT colonography every 5 years; or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, with or without FIT.A
The updated ACP guidance challenges the benefit of screening ages 45-49 and restricts recommended screening tests to colonoscopy or biennial faecal occult bood or immunohistochemical testing. A
Most guidelines in high resource economies recommend FIT testing every other year beginning at age 50 years. A
Most guidelines in high resource economies recommend FIT testing every other year beginning at age 50 years.

USPSTF: The 2021 recommendation statement from the USPSTF recommends screening average-risk adults age 50 to 75 years (A recommendation) using any of the following: annual FOBTs, annual FIT test; FIT-DNA every 1 to 3 years; colonoscopy every 10 years; CT colonography every 5 years; or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, with or without FIT. They also recommend screening adults age 45 to 49 (B recommendation) and considering screening in adults 75 to 85 years (C recommendation). Modeling studies commissioned by the USPSTF confirm that any approach to screening provides a large benefit in terms of life years gained (approximately 240-270 years per 1000 persons; ).

American College of Physicians: ACP guidelines are generally in agreement, adding that colonoscopy is preferred in higher risk patients and screening should begin earlier (age 40 years) in high risk patients. Updated ACP guidelines acknowledge the discrepant recommendations in existence with little to choose between different screening options and propose that screening should be undertaken using the test the patient chooses on the basis of information provided. They recommend screening age 50-75 years with biennial FIT or FOBT, or colonoscopy every 10 years, or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years with a biennial FIT. Updated guidance (2023) from the ACP challenges the existing USPSTF recommendations suggesting questionable benefit for screening in patients aged 45-49 years of average population risk. They also advise against use of stool DNA as a tool. B

American Cancer Society: ACS recommends screening average-risk adults age 45-75 using any of the following: annual FIT test, annual HS-gFOBT, FIT-DNA every 3 years, colonosocpy every 10 years, CT colonography every 5 years or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years.

US Multi-Society Task Force: This group of gastroenterology specialty societies recommends colonoscopy every 10 years and annual FIT (for those who decline colonoscopy) as "Tier 1" screening tests. They recommend FIT + fecal DNA (Cologuard) every 3 years. CT colonography every 5 years, and flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 to 10 years as "Tier 2" tests. They specifically recommend against use of the Septin9 serum assay, a biomarker blood test. Screening should begin at age 50 (45 in African-Americans) and continue until age 75 or life expectancy is less than 10 years. Based on expert opinion and limited quality observational data, they recommend colonoscopy every 5 years for persons at elevated risk due to family history, defined as advanced adenoma or CRC in a family member under 60 years of age or 2 or more family members with the same.

UK guidelines: UK guidelines for screening and surveillance in persons with high-risk familial polyposis syndromes are shown in UK guidelines classifies as high-risk patients with 2+ premalignant polyps at least one of which is advanced. Advanced is defined as being ≥10 mm or with high-grade dysplasia; a serrated polyp ≥10 mm, or with dysplasia. Also high risk were persons with 5+ premalignant polyps, or who have a single large (≥20 mm) non-pedunculated polyp. These patients should undergo surveillance colonoscopy at 3 years.

A systematic review of interventions to improve screening adherence found that mailed outreach including a FIT (or gFOBT) test was most effective, while education and patient navigators were less effective.
There is a risk of 'over-screening' due to lack of guidance on when to stop screening or overuse of colonoscopy outside of the standard framework of age and frequency for screening.

Population based analysis of outcomes from 'screening' colonoscopies suggests that 17-25% performed in US have no clear indication as per guidelines and that this overuse contributes to significant numbers of complications including approximately 2000 bowel perforations and 8000 severe bleeds per year..

The low likelihood of positive findings after an initial negative colonoscopy suggest that the rescreening interval could safely be extended beyond 10 years, although currently all guidelines still recommend a 10 year interval.
There continue to be recommendations without robust evidence for extending age range of screening.
A recent trial of a personalised decision tool to promote screening showed increased uptake in higher risk patients and appears promising.

The NORDICC trial randomized 94,959 healthy men and women, aged 55 to 64 years, from the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and Poland who had not previously been screened for CRC to colonoscopy or usual care. After 10 years median follow-up, the absolute reduction in risk (ARR) in CRC incidence was only 0.22%,number needed to invite (NNI) of 455 to detect one additional cancer. There was no reduction in CRC mortality in the primary analysis. An adjusted per protocol analysis found a lower incidence of CRC (0.84% vs 1.22%; RR 0.69; 0.55 - 0.83; NNI = 263) and a greater reduction in CRC mortality (0.15% vs 0.30%; RR 0.50; 0.27 - 0.77; NNI = 667). These reductions in CRC mortality are far lower than those modeled by the USPSTF for a lifetime of screening (ARR ˜ 2.5%).

Preliminary findings from an Italian RCT suggest that the yield of adenomas and cancers is similar between FIT every 2 years, colonoscopy, or colonography. Fecal DNA + FIT is expensive, with no data regarding clinical outcomes. Modeling studies suggesting that the lower specificity will lead to more colonoscopies than FIT alone.

There is a 60% mortality reduction from CRC for persons with polyps in reach of the sigmoidoscope. An unblinded RCT found that a single flexible sigmoidoscopy at age 60 years reduced the incidence of colorectal cancer (number needed to invite to screening = 3100). Results from the PLCO trial (n = 77,445 patients) found that patients randomized to flex sig had a reduced incidence of colorectal cancer and lower cancer-specific mortality due to distal disease after a median of 12 years of follow-up.

A large Spanish randomized trial (n = 57,404) comparing FIT (fecal immunochemical test or FIT) with colonoscopy has recently reported ten year follow up (COLONPREV trial). having previously reported 2 year follow-up results on acceptability of the two methods. Only a small number of cancers were detected overall but on the non-inferiority design of the trial the results suggest a similar benefit from both methods of screening.

In a National Cancer Institute RCT (n = 5999), an outreach program designed to increase screening for colon cancer demonstrated higher completion rates in the colonoscopy outreach group versus FIT outreach group versus usual care, 38.4% versus 28% versus 10.7% respectively and higher detection rates of adenomas and advanced neoplasias in the colonoscopy and FIT outreach groups when compared to usual care. However, detection rates of adenomas and advanced neoplasias were higher in the colonoscopy outreach group versus the FIT outreach group; 17.8% higher for detection of adenoma and 3.7% higher for detection of advanced neoplasia.

An RCT (n = 2245) performed at a large academic system studied incentives for CRC screening with colonoscopy. The three groups compared were people who received an email with a phone number to schedule a colonoscopy, email with an active choice to opt in or out of a colonoscopy and email with an active choice to opt in or out plus a $100 incentive. The rates of colonoscopy completion were highest in the opt in/out email with incentive. 1.6%, 1.5% and 3.7% respectively (p = 0.01).

In a Norwegian study, these investigators randomly invited individuals aged 50 to 74 years (N = 139,291) for either a once-only screening flexible sigmoidoscopy or a fecal immunochemical test (FIT) every other year for a maximum of 4 rounds. Every-other-year FIT, over at least 6 years, identified fewer cancers or advanced adenomas initially but caught up and surpassed a single sigmoidoscopy after 3 rounds of testing. The increased detection might be in part due to the greater participation in FIT than sigmoidoscopy.

A randomized trial of 4459 men living with HIV who were screened for high grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) caused by HPV found that immediate treatment reduced the progression of these lesions to invasive anal cancer.

A trial randomized 3523 volunteers to a single free colonoscopy or to annual fecal occult blood test with a high sensitivity guaic test (hsFOBT). Adherence to any participation was higher with colonoscopy (84% vs 73%, p < .001), and full adherence to all 5 years of hsFOBT was low (38%). Detection rates for adenomas or serrated lesions was higher with colonoscopy. These results should be interpreted cautiously - the more important comparison would be mortality and cancer incidence rates over a longer period.

Colonoscopy is better at detecting adenomatous polyps than double contrast barium enema (39%). An interval of 10 years following normal exam is acceptable; a study found no cancers and only 1% with advanced polyps 5 years after a previous normal colonoscopy. Two nonrandomized trials have reported the benefits of screening colonoscopy in asymptomatic adults. An observational study of high risk patients (all with blood in stool, positive FOBT, or family history) found that colonoscopy approximately halved the death rate due to colorectal cancer compared with the general population. Another observational study found a reduction in CRC specific mortality and CRC incidence in persons who chose to undergo flex sig or colonoscopy. The adjusted hazard ratio was 0.32 for colonoscopy (95% CI 0.24-0.45) and 0.59 for flex sign (95% CI 0.45-0.76). Risk of colonoscopy is perforation in 1 in 500 and death in 1 in 5000.

The NORDICC trial randomized 94,959 healthy men and women, aged 55 to 64 years, from the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and Poland who had not previously been screened for CRC to colonoscopy or usual care. After 10 years median follow-up, the absolute reduction in risk (ARR) in CRC incidence was only 0.22%,number needed to invite (NNI) of 455 to detect one additional cancer. There was no reduction in CRC mortality in the primary analysis. An adjusted per protocol analysis found a lower incidence of CRC (0.84% vs 1.22%; RR 0.69; 0.55 - 0.83; NNI = 263) and a greater reduction in CRC mortality (0.15% vs 0.30%; RR 0.50; 0.27 - 0.77; NNI = 667). These reductions in CRC mortality are far lower than those modeled by the USPSTF for a lifetime of screening (ARR ˜ 2.5%).

Analysis of all current screening methods using Markov modeling suggests that colonoscopy is the most effective strategy in improving outcomes. Delay in proceedings with colonoscopy following positive FIT screening more than 6 months is associated with an increased risk of advanced stage cancer at diagnosis.
Any polyps should be removed. Polypectomy significantly decreases the incidence of CRC.

Advanced adenomas (adenoma greater than or equal to 1 cm with high grade dysplasia, tubovillous or villous histology) increase the risk of CRC compared to no adenomas found on colonoscopy (2.9% incidence of CRC over 15 years versus 1.2%).
Nonadvanced adenoma defined as less than 1 cm and no advanced histology, one or two nonadvanced adenomas versus three or more nonadvanced ademonas show no difference in rate of CRC incidence. B

Persons with no adenoma compared to a low risk adenoma (1 or 2 tubular adenomas, <1 cm, no high grade dysplasia and average risk of CRC) on initial colonoscopy had lower likelihood of advanced adenoma at five year follow up colonoscopy (3.3% vs 4.9%) A

Another systematic review found that the prevalence of advanced neoplasia following negative index colonoscopy was 2.8% between 1 and 5 years later, 3.2% between 5 and 10 years later, and 7.0% more than 10 years later, supporting a 10 year screening interval as adequate.

A 2023 review of 120,000 screening colonoscopies from a German population registry demonstrates that increasing the interval from a negative colonoscopy from 10 years to more than 14 years makes only a minor difference in detection rate for invasive malignancy. This constitues level Ib evidence and may prompt review of current guidelines on interval for screening.

A review of over 165,000 colonoscopies performed in a Polish population aged 50-66 years has shown that with a well prepared colonoscopy a negative result predicted for low risk of malignancy for significantly longer than 10 years and up to 17 years. This does raise the question as to how often the screening needs to be.
Adenoma detection rate decreases at the end of the day and withdrawal time for colonoscopy decreases throughout the day

In over 1600 adults undergoing colonoscopy, a randomized trial found that a low-volume same-day polyethylene glycol–based bowel preparation (15 mg bisacodyl the afternoon before and 2 liters of PEG 4 to 5 hours before the procedure) was as effective as either a low-volume or high-volume split-dose preparation.

A meta-analysis of 19 studies demonstrated sensitivity of 82% and specificity of 94% for FIT with no difference observed between the different commerical products. In patients with a family or personal history of CRC, a systematic review of 12 studies with over 6000 patients found that FIT was 93% sensitive and 91% specific for detection of cancer (LR+ 10, LR− 0.08). For advanced neoplasia, though, sensitivity was only 48% and specificity 93% (LR+ 7, LR− 0.57).

A meta-analysis of 9 studies demonstrated that quantitative FIT (cut off 10 µg Hb/g) can be used in patients with lower abdominal symptoms without rectal bleeding who do not meet criteria for colonoscopy to rule out CRC, which supports the NICE DG 30 guidelines. However, more research is needed on the types of quantitatve FIT

A meta-analysis of 31 studies n= 120,255 provides high level evidence for both sensitivity and specificty of FIT single test using different cut-offs to rule out or rule in CRC. A cutoff of <10 mcg/g is good at ruling out CRC (LR- 0.1) while a value >20 mcg/g is good at increasing the likelihood of CRC (LR+ 15.5).

A study utilizing microsimulation assessed cost-effectiveness and life years gained of FIT versus FIT plus colonoscopy versus no screening or surveillance demonstrated that FIT and FIT plus colonoscopy at scheduled intervals of 5 or 10 years were more cost effective and had more life year gained than no screening or surveillance.
Similarly, a study in the Veneto region of Italy found that the detection rate for CRC after 5 rounds of biennial FIT is similar to that in published studies of colonoscopy.

The sensitivity of FIT is not affected by taking low-dose aspirin. Similarly, a systematic review found that NSAIDs, low dose aspirin, and anticoagulants do not affect the positive predictive value of FIT used as a screening test.

This test (Cologuard) is expensive ($600), with no data regarding clinical outcomes. Modeling studies suggesting that the lower specificity will lead to more colonoscopies than FIT alone.In a direct comparison of FIT with fecal DNA (that incorporated a FIT test), the fecal DNA had a higher sensitivity but lower specificity. The positive predictive value was better for FIT (9.2% vs 4.6%), resulting in fewer follow-up colonoscopies per cancer detected for FIT (22 vs 11).

The BLUE-C trial compared fecal DNA + FIT to FIT alonein 26,758 adults 40 and older scheduled for colonoscopy of whom just over 20,000 provided usable data for accuracy compared with the reference standard of colonoscopy. This study evaluated an updated version of the Cologuard test. Sensitivity for cancer (93.9% vs 67.3%) and advanced adenoma (43.4% vs 23.3%) for the fecal DNA + FIT test, but specificity for advanced neoplasia was lower (90.6% vs 94.8%). This would result in more false positives. The impact on mortality is unknown.

10,000 people need to complete FOBT screening to prevent 8.5 deaths from CRC over 10 years (number needed to screen = 1173). However, FOBT on stool samples obtained by digital rectal examination (DRE) does not reduce mortality.
Accuracy of CT colonography is improving. A recent study found that virtual colonoscopy was able to detect large polyps even without a bowel prep.
Septin9 and PillCam colon are not currently recommended for CRC screening.

There is increasing focus on the use of circulating tumour DNA as a screening approach but in a recent study of over 30,000 asymptomatic individuals the moderate sensitivity (82%) and specificity (91%) for detection of invasive cancer was negated by the poor 12% sensitivity for advanced adenoma/in situ/dysplasia changes. On this basis this method is not recommended for general screening.
FIT versus gFOBT: non-randomized control trial demonstrated rates of advanced adenoma and CRC were higher with FIT versus gFOBT (1.29% and 0.24% v 0.35% and 0.12% respectively). B
FIT and gFOBT have similar specificities 96.8%-98.6% however sensitivities differed between the type of FIT testing and gFOBT test in one study (n = 1006)
Antioxidant supplementation does not decrease risk for CRC or polyps.
The role of dietary fiber remains controversial and a recent meta-analysis does suggest an inverse correlation between fiber consumption and risk of both proximal and distal colon cancer.

An analysis of recent primary prevention trials of aspirin versus placebo in the context of widespread screening for colorectal cancer found no reduction in cancer incidence or mortality with aspirin. However, a recent meta-analysis suggesting aspirin does reduce risk of colorectal cancer but with number needed to treat as high as 931 taking all studies with all doses of aspirin. However for high dose aspirin >500mg per day the benefit was clearer (NNT=60) but at the expense of increased gastrointestinal toxicity.A
Aspirin does have proven efficacy in preventing colorectal cancer in Lynch syndrome carriers, established on the 20 year follow-up of a controlled trial in this population.
For patients who are overweight or obese, losing weight may decrease the risk of dying from CRC.

A systematic review of all studies of dietary intervention concluded that most studies were small, poor methodology prevailed and outcomes defined were often clinically irrelevant. In 252 studies of over 30,000 patients it was not possible to draw robust conclusions.
Estrogen decreases the risk of colon cancer, but there was an increased risk of more advanced colon cancer developing in women who took estrogen.

Calcium and vitamin D may decrease the risk of colonic polyps, but the effect on CRC is unknown. Folic acid and antioxidants do not reduce the risk of colorectal adenomas. Daily multivitamin supplements in men do not reduce the risk of colorectal cancer.
Statins may decrease the risk of CRC.
Calcium supplementation reduces the risk of polyp recurrence (NNT = 14.3).
Dietary fiber supplementation does not prevent recurrence of polyps.
Aspirin and NSAIDs decrease the risk for polyp recurrence (NNT = 12.5; 95% CI 7.7-25.0).
An RCT of 417 adults treated surgically for digestive cancer found no increase in relapse-free survival with vitamin D supplementation (2000 IU daily).
Signs and symptoms vary with size of lesion and location, and include bleeding, constipation, unexpected weight loss, and anemia. C
Patients younger than 40 with rectal bleeding have a CRC risk of less than 1%. A
Colonoscopy with biopsy for tissue diagnosis examines the entire colon and is the preferred initial test for patients with suspected colon cancer. C

Rectal bleeding has a PV+ of 8.1% for colorectal cancer in patients aged 50 years or older. The PV+ for abdominal pain is 3.3%, and for anemia 9.7%. The LR+ for rectal bleeding plus weight loss or change in bowel habit was 1.9. Abdominal pain, diarrhea, and constipation plus rectal bleeding were not helpful. In general, though, symptoms are unreliable.
Fecal incontinence,tenesmus, rectal mucus, and change in flatus are other significant but less common symptoms of CRC.
CRC is uncommon in patients younger than 40 without risk factors (<1% of those who present with bleeding).

A study of patients age 18 to 49 years in the US VA Health System identified a 5 year cumulative incidence of 0.45% among persons with iron deficiency anemia and 0.33% among persons presenting with hematochezia. Colonoscopy should be considered in the absence of a clearly identified cause of bleeding, especially in persons over age 30 years. The risk difference was greater for men than for women.
Patients with right-sided adenocarcinoma may present with a palpable abdominal mass.

Consider CRC in patients with unexplained anemia. A study of adults with anemia found CRC in 6% with serum ferritin <50 ng/mL, 2.3% with ferritin between 50 and 100 ng/mL, and only 0.9% with ferritin greater than 100 ng/mL.

In patients with an episode of diverticulitis, evaluation for colorectal cancer is only indicated for patients with complicated disease (i.e., fistula, abscess, perforation). In patients with uncomplicated disease only 0.5% had colorectal cancer, compared with 8.3% with complicated disease.
Anoscopy is limited to rectal lesions, while flexible sigmoidoscopy can examine and biopsy distal lesions.
Colonoscopy with biopsy for tissue diagnosis examines the entire colon and is the preferred initial test for patients with suspected colon cancer.
Transrectal ultrasound can determine the extent of involvement of rectal lesions.
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is used in postoperative management of CRC but is not a reliable diagnostic test.
Fecal occult blood testing, although useful for screening, is not accurate in diagnostic work-up for those with symptoms.
CT is used to determine the extent of metastases; a thickened colonic mucosa on CT scan is an indication for colonoscopy.
PET scan is used for staging in patients with liver metastases.
FDG-PET scan is useful for detecting invasive CRC proximal to an obstructing CRC.

CT colonography and MR colonography have similar sensitivities, specificities and negative likelihood ratio for diagnosis of CRC. CT colonography had much higher positive likelihood ratio compared to MR colonography.
NICE guidelines recommend CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis to stage the disease in all patients with colorectal cancer.
Incidental finding of a focal PET avid lesion in the colon while investigating other pathology requires upgent colonoscopy as it carries positive predictive value of almost 50% for advanced CRC.

Guidelines from Great Britain and Ireland provides guidance regarding using quantitative FIT testing as a way to triage adults with symptoms suspicious for colorectal cancer. Urgent investigation is recommended for those with fecal hemoglobin >= 10 micrograms Hb/gram. Patients with a value < 10 but with persistent or ongoing symptoms of concern should be referred routinely or urgently based on physician judgement.
A clinical decision rule can be used to identify patients at very low risk of advanced proximal CRC in patients who have had a flexible sigmoidoscopy. This score has been prospectively validated.
Signs and symptoms vary with size of lesion and location.
Patients younger than 40 with rectal bleeding have a CRC risk of less than 1%.
Include abdominal palpation and DRE in the physical examination. Anoscopy is useful to evaluate bright red rectal bleeding.
Colonoscopy has the highest single-test accuracy for evaluation of the colon.
Surgical resection is the primary treatment for CRC.A
In advanced CRC, chemotherapy and radiation therapy are often used as adjuvant therapy. A
Adjuvant chemotherapy is recommended for selected patients with T3 or T4 CRC. It is of less certain benefit for patients with lower stage CRC.A
Chinese herbs (Huangqi compounds) decrease nausea, vomiting, and leukopenia secondary to chemotherapy for CRC.
Vitamin D supplementation does not improve relapse free survival in adults with digestive tract cancer, including colorectal cancer.
A Cochrane review of 20 studies found that certain herbal medicines may improve outcomes when combined with chemotherapy.
A randomized trial compared a standardized dose of green tea extract with placebo in 879 patients found no efffect on the likelihood of colon adenomas.
Consider consultation for tissue confirmation, determination of extent of disease, and necessity of genetic counseling in patients with suspected hereditary syndromes.
Consider hospitalization for complications related to CRC: perforation, obstruction, malnutrition, and severe anemia.
A Cochrane review found, based on very limited evidence, that corticosteroids may hasten resolution of bowel obstruction associated with colorectal cancer.
Admit for complications related to chemotherapy, e.g., sepsis.

Surgical resection is the primary treatment for CRC. Laparoscopic colorectal resection has short-term benefits compared with conventional colorectal resection, with no difference in morbidity or mortality. However, it may not be as cost effective.

Laproscopic surgery has a shorter time to post-op flatus, less post-op complications and a shorter hospital stay than conventional open surgery. There was no difference in the number of lymph nodes retrieved in the meta-analysis. However, long term usefulness was not analyzed in this study.
Low rectal cancer may require permanent colostomy. Cancer above the rectum often does not require a permanent colostomy.
High ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) in patients with CRC may increase overall survival but a high powered well designed RCT needs to be completed
There is a clear difference in the quality of life of people who undergo anterior resection versus abdominoperineal excision for rectal cancer.

Total mesorectal excision is the surgical technique of choice for rectal cancer. A Cochrane review comparing laparoscopic with open TME found moderate quality evidence that outcomes were similar with both but with better short term recovery with laparoscopic intervention.
For patients undergoing low rectal resection and coloanal anastamosis, colonic J pouch was superior in RCTs to straight coloanal anastamosis.

For patients presenting as emergencies with obstruction, it is not clear whether the outcome is better with a staged approach to address obstruction followed by surgery to the primary tumour, or to undertake a single operation. A Cochrane review was unable to find evidence to address this issue.
Chewing gum improves bowel mobility and reduces length of stay following colorectal surgery.
There is no evidence that mechanical bowel preparation prevents leakage or infectious complications during surgery for CRC.
A systematic review of 9 studies found insufficient evidence that stapling was superior to hand sewing for colorectal anastamosis.
Higher volume for surgeons (and to a lesser extent for hospitals) is associated with lower rates of mortality and permanent stoma.

A randomized trial of 4459 men living with HIV who were screened for high grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) caused by HPV found that immediate treatment (excision or topical) reduced the likelihood of progression of these lesions to invasive anal cancer.
Capecitabine, a prodrug of 5-FU, has an improved response rate compared with 5-FU and less toxicity.

The optimal duration of adjuvant chemotherapy has been recently assessed with over 12,000 patients, comparing FOLFOX (5FU, Leucovorin and oxaliplatin) and CAPOX (capecitabine and oxaliplatin). For FOLFOX the non-inferiority of 3 months duration treatment against 6 months was not confirmed, i.e. 6 months remains better. However, for the CAPOX regimen it appears that 3 months treatment is noninferior to 6 months.

In a meta-analysis of 13 studies, comparison was made between oxaliplatin +/- bevacizumab and irinotecan +/- bevacizumab and although there was no survival difference between the two regimens, the oxaliplatin treatment gave a higher overal response rate and had less toxicity.

Cetuximab and bevacizumab are monoclonal antibodies used with multidrug regimens. Short- and long-duration infusions with paclitaxel are similarly effective, based on a Cochrane systematic review. Adverse outcomes appeared to be increased with longer infusions, especially in women. The quality of evidence was weak, though.

A trial identified 115 patients with locally advanced but non-metastatic, previously untreated mismatch repair-deficient CRC and treated them with neoadjuvant nivolumab + ipilimumab prior to surgery. All but 2 underwent timely surgery, and a major pathological response with less than 10% residual tumor was seen in 105 of 115 patients (95%).

Circulating tumor (ct) DNA post-operatively may have value in guiding therapy; patients with ctDNA detected have decreased rates of recurrence free survival. A trial randomized 455 patients with stage II colorectal cancer in a 2:1 ratio to ctDNA guided therapy or usual care and followed them for a median of 37 months. A positive ctDNA at 4 or 7 weeks post-operatively prompted oxaliplatin-based or fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy. Fewer patients in the ctDNA guided group received chemotherapy, but with no difference in the rate of recurrence-free survival (93.5% vs 92.4%).
Radiation therapy reduces the risk of local recurrence by 20% to 25% in patients with rectal cancer.
Consider partial liver resection (5-year mortality rate 25%-35%) in patients with solitary liver metastases.
For patients presenting with synchronous liver metastases, a systematic review found no difference in outcome between initial bowel surgery, initial liver surgery or both simultaneously.

A recent review of patient outcomes from the SEER database of 37,793 patients with metastatic CRC evaluated benefit of primary tumour resection. This demonstrated significant overall and cancer specific survival for resection of primary tumour even in presence of metastatic disease.
Chemotherapy is effective at improving survival in patients with advanced CRC. It is of less certain benefit for patients with lower stage CRC.
Fluorouracil (5-FU) is an important drug for advanced CRC, often given with leucovorin, which modulates its activity.
Oxaliplatin may be used as treatment in combination with 5-FU and leucovorin in both adjuvant and metastatic settings (NICE guidelines).

A systematic review of 7 RCTs with 3680 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer demonstrated improved progression free survival, overall survival, and response rate in those treated with biological therapy in addition to standard FOLFIRI chemotherapy without an increase in adverse events.

A study identified 492 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer who had received up to 2 previous rounds of chemotherapy. They were randomized to trifluridine–tipiracil (FTD–TPI) or FTD-TPI plus bevacizumab. The median overall survival was significantly longer in the combination therapy group (10.8 vs 7.5 months) with a HR for mortality of 0.61 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.54). The time to worsening of performance status score was also slowed by about 3 months in the combination therapy group.

A trial recruited 303 patients with microsatellite-instability-high metastatic CRC and randomized them in a 2:2:1 ratio to nivolumab+ipilimumab, nivolumab alone, or chemotherapy with or without targetted therapies. After 31 months, progression free survival was better in the nivolumab+ipilimumab group than chemotherapy (24 month PFS 72% vs 14%). Results for the comparison w ith nivolumab alone or overall survival are not yet reported.

In heavily pretreated patients with metastatic colorectal cancer and the mutant KRAS G12C gene, a small Phase 1/2 RCT found that combination therapy with adagrasib and cetuximab provided modest benefit compared with adagrasib alone in terms of progression free survival.

A study randomized 637 patients with BRAF-mutated metastatic CRC to encorafenib + cetuximab (EC), EC+mFOLFOX6, or usual care (largely bevacizumab+chemotherapy). Overall survival was longer with EC+mFOLFOX6 than usual care (30.3 vs 15.1 months, p < .001).

A trial randomized 160 patients with refractory CRC and mutated KRAS G12C to sotorasib 960 mg once daily + panitumumab, sotorasib 240 mg once daily + panitumumab, or the investigator’s choice of trifluridine–tipiracil or regorafenib. Progression free survival after 8 months was 5.6 months, 3.9 months, and 2.2 months respectively. Overall survival data were not yet available.
Irinotecan is a topoisomerase inhibitor that is used for metastatic CRC.

Optimal duration of chemotherapy in advanced disease remains uncertain but a large RCT (n = 558) suggests increased progression free survival with use of maintenance chemotherapy following an initial six cycles of capecitabine and bevacizumab.

tr.th: Year to start, interval, and duration

tr.td: Lynch Syndrome, MLH1 and MSH2 gene carriers
25 years, every 2 years until 75
Lynch Syndrome, MSH6 and PMS2 gene carriers
35 years, every 2 years till age 75
Lynch-like Syndrome
25 years, every 2 years till age 75
Serrated polyposis syndrome
From age of diagnosis, then every 1-2 years until age 75
Serrated polyposis syndrome, first degree relatives
Age 40 or 10 years before index ccase, then every 5 years till age 75 years
Multiple colorectal adenomas (10 + without pathogenic variants in APC or MUTYH)
From age at diagnosis, then every 1 to 2 years till age 75 years
Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
12 to 14 years, then every 1-3 years
Also perform EGD beginning age 25 if APC pathogenic variant carrier
MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP)
18 to 20 years, then annually
Also perform EGD starting age 35
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS)
15 years, then every 1-3 years based on the patient's phenotype.
Juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS), SMAD4 and BMPR1A pathogenic variant carriers
18 years, then every 1-3 years depending on phenotype.
If SMAD4 variant, EGD starting 18 and every 1-3 years. If BMPR1A variant, EGD starting 25 and every 1-3 years.
